newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch budget seen slashing EMU debt/GDP ratio.
newsitem.headline: Dutch budget seen slashing EMU debt/GDP ratio.

text.p: Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm is expected to pull an ace from his sleeve and cut public sector debt sharply when he unveils the 1997 budget on Tuesday.

Economists and the parliamentary press confidently predict he will slash about two percentage points off the debt to GDP ratio -- the only criterion for European economic and monetary union (EMU) which has posed a problem for the Netherlands.
Several pundits believe Zalm will use government cash reserves held by the central bank to reduce public debt while others expect the government to sell land or company shares.
Economists note that Dutch inflation and interest rates have long been among the lowest in the European Union and that the guilder is one of its strongest and most stable currencies.
The public sector deficit has fallen steadily in recent years and is tipped to fall well below the EMU threshold of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) next year.
By contrast Dutch public sector debt started to edge lower only recently after mushrooming in the 1970s and 1980s.
But Zalm told parliament in May that the 1996 debt ratio had been revised upwards as a result of higher levels of debt among local government bodies and social security funds.
The revised figure put the debt ratio at 79.6 percent of GDP, down only 0.2 percentage points from 1995 and well above the EMU target level of 60 percent of GDP.

Zalm has long insisted that the debt ratio figure should show a substantial decline "before the decimal point", arguing that if this were achieved the Dutch would sail through their EMU exams because they have scored well on all other measures.
He now seems to have convinced the cabinet of the need to cut the debt ratio and, while nobody claims to know exactly what he has up his sleeve, there is broad agreement on its effect.
"On balance, we expect the cabinet to take sufficient additional measures to reduce the debt ratio to 77.5 percent of GDP or even less in 1997," said Bob Kommers of ABN AMRO Bank.
Fred Pallada at ING Bank said it was not wrong to resort to creative measures to reduce the debt ratio.
"Some call this a trick but the method is completely legitimate," he said in the bank's economic review Infograph.
To a large extent Zalm's job has been made easier this year by the Netherlands' relatively robust economic performance.
GDP grew at a year-on-year rate of 2.8 percent in the second quarter and job growth has led to falling unemployment.
This brought a rare accolade from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer this week but has also generated extra tax revenues.
Zalm is expected to cut the lowest income tax rate but this will probably be offset by higher social security charges to help plug welfare fund deficits.
Press reports say the real purchasing power of most consumers will be kept steady in 1997 with a small increase in purchasing power for the poorest groups.
Home-owners are expected to win a reduction in taxes paid to central government which will roughly offset an earlier hike in taxes paid to local government.
Taxes levied on cigarettes and petrol are both tipped to rise but road tax will be lowered in an attempt to persuade motorists to use their cars less frequently.
In addition to the 1997 budget, the government will also present a discussion document next Tuesday on the future of the Dutch social security system.

Government sources said this would focus on making the labour market more flexible, reducing dependence on welfare benefits and ensuring the state pension scheme (AOW) can be maintained as the average age of the population rises.
